html:
Surah Al-Mulk (The Sovereignty) is the 67th chapter of the Qur’an — thirty short verses revealed in Makkah. The sahabah knew it by three other names: Tabarak, from its opening word; Al-Māniʿah, “The Preventer”; and Al-Munjiyah, “The Rescuer.” Imam al-Tirmidhī records that the Prophet (✌) said, “There is a surah of the Qur’an of thirty verses that interceded for a man until he was forgiven — it is Surah Tabārak alladhī bi-yadihi’l-mulk” (Jamiʿ at-Tirmidhī 2891, graded hasan by al-Tirmidhī, authenticated by Ibn Hibbān and al-Hākim, and classed hasan by Shaykh al-Albānī). This is one of the best-supported virtues attached to any single surah in the Sunnah.

The surah’s most famous nickname — The Preventer — comes from a statement of Ibn Masʿūd (ra), recorded by al-Hākim and al-Ṭabarānī through Sufyān ath-Thawrī: that angels will approach a man in his grave from every side, and each limb that recited Surah al-Mulk will refuse them entry (al-Mustadrak 3839). The muhaddithūn note that this report is mawqūf — a statement of the sahabi himself, not a direct quotation of the Prophet — and the longer version attributed to the Prophet through ʿArfajah is layyin (weak). The virtue remains established; the attribution is honest.

Ibn Kathīr, in his tafsir, points out that the surah’s central argument is Allah’s absolute dominion over everything — life, death, the seven heavens, every bird that spreads its wings, and every secret kept in the chest. Verses 3 and 4 issue a direct invitation: “So look again — do you see any flaw? Then look again, and again — your sight will return to you humbled and worn out.” The Qur’an is asking the reader to actually inspect the sky, not just believe a claim about it. This is why the surah has been a favourite of scientists, poets, and ordinary readers across fourteen centuries: it rewards contemplation.

If you are reading this at qurandaily.org, the recommended practice is to recite Surah al-Mulk every night before sleeping — Jabir (ra) reports that the Prophet (✌) would not sleep until he had recited it (Tirmidhī 2892). It takes about four minutes. For memorisation, one verse per day finishes the entire surah inside a single month.
